questions.q: Futures contracts to short (ignoring basis drift):
questions.why: β-weighted exposure = 1.1×500 Cr = 550 Cr; contract value = 20,300×75 = Rs 15.225 lakh; N = 550×10^7 / 15.225×10^5 ≈ 3,612. Forgetting β gives 3,284; using spot 20,000 gives 3,666 Forgetting beta or the futures basis produces the other counts.

questions.stem: A fund holds Rs 500 crore of an equity index portfolio (β 1.1) and fears a short-term dip; index future lot 75 units at index 20,000; 3-month futures 20,300. Alternatives: buy index puts at strike 19,800 (premium 340 index pts) or sell index calls at 20,600 receiving 180 pts. The desk decides to collar.

questions.q: Selling index futures changes the portfolio's value with a 1% index fall (index drops, futures gain):
o: ~Flat: futures profit offsets the β-weighted loss
questions.why: A β-matched short futures position gains ≈ what the portfolio loses (5.5 Cr each on a 1% fall), leaving basis and tail risk — the fall is insured and the upside surrendered.
questions.trend: No dominant past-pattern signal; included for balanced coverage (AI judgement).
questions.probWhy: Lower likelihood but possible — this topic stays active in ICAI question-setting Included so a low-probability surprise cannot catch you cold.

mem.tip: Hedged ≠ riskless — basis remains A short hedge mops the floor while blocking the view of the sunshine.

questions.q: Buying puts (strike 19,800; premium 340) caps the downside floor at:
questions.why: Net floor = strike − premium = 19,800 − 340 = 19,460 index points; below the put strike the payoff mirrors the decline; above, full participation minus premium.
questions.trend: Repeated theme in recent ICAI exam question-patterns for this paper (AI pattern estimate — not a citation to a specific past paper question).
questions.probWhy: HIGH likelihood for Nov 2026 — this topic stays active in ICAI question-setting Prediction is study guidance, not an ICAI statement.

mem.tip: The net-floor arithmetic is the whole question Insurance pays from the deductible: your floor is strike minus premium.

questions.q: The collar's cost and bands: put 340 out, call 180 in ⇒
questions.why: Net premium = 340 − 180 = 160 pts; payoff band between the strikes; the short call's cap surrenders index moves beyond 20,600 — trading upside for cheap protection.

mem.tip: Collar = band + net premium A collar borrows from the ceiling to pay for the floor: cheap, and it pins the room's height.

questions.q: If the desk also holds an expected dividend of 0.6% before expiry, the futures fair value relative to spot is (3-m, rf 6.5%):
questions.why: Cost-of-carry F = S(1+(r−q)t): (6.5−0.6)% × 0.25 = 1.475% premium — dividends shave the carry but do not flip it to a discount unless the yield exceeds the rate.

mem.tip: Carry net of dividends Dividends pull futures toward the cash — carry counts net of the payout.

questions.q: S = Rs 120, strike Rs 120, one-year risk-free discount factor 1.0513 (continuous 5%), European call premium Rs 14. Parity implies the European put is closest to:
questions.why: C + K·e^(−rt) = P + S ⇒ P = 14 − 120 + 120/1.0513 = 14 − 120 + 114.15 = Rs 8.15. Skipping the discount (14 − 120 + 120 = 14) and sign-flipping are the standard wrong turns.

mem.tip: Call minus stock plus discounted strike = put. The discount is the whole exam.

questions.q: Holding a stock and buying a put on it is:
o: Protective put portfolio insurance — floor below, upside retained
questions.why: Protective put = long asset + long put: loss capped below strike (plus premium cost), upside kept.

mem.tip: A put under your shares is a floor under the floor: pay the premium, keep the sky.

questions.q: A call has delta 0.6. The delta-neutral stock holding per call option short is:
o: Hold 0.6 shares per short call (delta hedge)
questions.why: Δ = 0.6 shares per option — short call ⇒ long 0.6 stock keeps net delta zero; re-hedge as Δ moves (gamma).
questions.trend: Fits the style in which ICAI drafts RTP/MTP questions on this topic (pattern estimate; no guarantee of appearance).
questions.probWhy: Lower likelihood but possible — delta-hedge ratios are concept-questions with tiny arithmetic Included so a low-probability surprise cannot catch you cold.

mem.tip: Δ shares per option short = delta; position size = Δ per contract.
